# Refrigeration A refrigerator pumps heat out of one place and dumps it somewhere else. It needs no freezer: a loop of pipe, a pump, radiators and an [textlink="expansion valve" link="KsFluidDevices"] will cool a room far below anything the air around you could.
## How it works It runs on a refrigerant: something that is a liquid at high pressure and a vapor at low pressure at the temperatures you care about. Ammonia is the easy one. - [bold]The compressor[/bold] squeezes the refrigerant vapor into the high side. Squeezing it raises its boiling point above the temperature outside. - [bold]The condenser[/bold] is a run of radiators somewhere you don't mind warming. The hot vapor gives up its heat there and condenses into liquid. - [bold]The expansion valve[/bold] lets that liquid into the low side, where its boiling point is far below the room's. - [bold]The evaporator[/bold] is a run of radiators in the room you want cold. The cold liquid boils inside them, taking the room's heat with it. - The compressor draws the vapor back off the evaporator, and round it goes.
## Building one 1. Lay a closed loop: compressor, condenser radiators, expansion valve, evaporator radiators, and back to the compressor's inlet. Gas flows from a pump's and a valve's inlet to their outlet, so mind which way they face. 2. Put the condenser where its heat can go: outside on lattice, in a big room, or out in space. 3. Put the evaporator in the room to cool. A sealed room cools fastest. 4. Charge the loop with refrigerant from a canister at a connector port. Keep it pure: no air in the loop. 5. Turn the compressor on, set the valve to hold its outlet pressure, and pick a pressure. The valve's window tells you what temperature that boils at.
The loop starts from nothing but vapor. Within a minute or so the condenser fills with liquid, the valve starts passing it, and the evaporator turns cold. Check with a gas analyzer: liquid in the condenser radiators, a cold evaporator, and the valve showing a steady flow mean it is working.
## Getting it right - [bold]Use a volume pump as the compressor.[/bold] A pressure pump empties the low side into near vacuum, which runs the evaporator far colder than you set and starves the valve. A volume pump draws a steady amount, as a real compressor does. - [bold]If the valve sits wide open and never reaches its pressure[/bold], the compressor is drawing more than the valve can feed. Turn the pump's rate down, or charge more refrigerant. - [bold]A condenser runs warmer than its surroundings.[/bold] That is how it gets rid of the heat, and it is why its liquid makes it to the valve. More condenser radiators let it run cooler and at a lower pressure. - [bold]A condenser can't be too hot.[/bold] Above a refrigerant's critical temperature nothing condenses, however hard you pump. Nitrous oxide's is barely above room temperature, so give it a condenser in space. Ammonia condenses comfortably in an ordinary room. - [bold]Pick the pump for the pressure.[/bold] Nitrous oxide needs more pressure than a pressure pump can give to condense at room temperature; a volume pump gets there. - [bold]Pressure falls along a run of radiators[/bold], so the far end of the evaporator runs colder than the valve says, and the far end of the condenser at a lower pressure. - [bold]An evaporator with nothing to cool floods.[/bold] Once the room is as cold as the evaporator, the liquid has no heat left to boil it and collects in the pipes. That is harmless: it boils again as soon as the room warms. - [bold]Don't freeze your refrigerant.[/bold] Ammonia and nitrous oxide freeze not far below their boiling points, so the far end of an evaporator can ice up. Ice in the evaporator doesn't flow, and stays until the pipe warms.
## Safety - [bold]Keep oxygen out of an ammonia loop.[/bold] Ammonia burns with oxygen once it is warm, and the high side of a loop is warm. - [bold]A broken loop spills its refrigerant.[/bold] Liquid ammonia boils off into the room as ammonia gas, which is harmful to breathe. - [bold]Pumps heat their room.[/bold] A powered compressor turns most of its heat back into electricity, but some still goes into the room it stands in. Keep it out of the room you are cooling.
## Moving heat between pipes Nothing moves heat straight from one pipe into another. To cool a pipe with your refrigerator, put its radiators and the evaporator's radiators together in a small sealed chamber, and let the chamber's air carry the heat between them.
## Liquefying gases A gas no refrigerator can condense, such as nitrogen, can still be liquefied by making it cool itself. Squeezed hard and let out through an expansion valve, nitrogen comes out a little colder than it went in. Send that cold gas back to chill the gas on its way to the valve, and each pass comes out colder than the last, until part of it comes out liquid. 1. Build a loop: a volume pump, a few radiators outside to shed its heat, a heat exchanger, and an expansion valve, returning through the heat exchanger to the pump. 2. Make the heat exchanger a column of small sealed chambers, one tile each, filled with a gas such as plasma. Run the high-pressure pipe down through every chamber with a radiator in each, and the returning pipe back up through them the other way, with its own radiator in each. 3. Charge the loop with nitrogen, run the pump at full rate, and set the valve to hold a low pressure. If the valve stays shut, there is too much nitrogen in the loop for the low side to reach its pressure.
It takes a while. The cold end creeps down a few degrees a minute, and liquid appears once the gas reaching the valve is about as cold as nitrogen's critical temperature. The liquid collects in the pipe after the valve. - [bold]One big chamber won't do.[/bold] It only brings both pipes to its own temperature. A column of them lets the cold end pull away from the warm end, and more chambers get colder.
